t.4.17.1: Then, struck by Rāma with an arrow, Vālī, harsh in battle, suddenly fell like a tree that has been cut down.
t.4.17.2: He, adorned with ornaments of refined gold, fell to the ground with all his limbs outstretched, like the banner of the king of the gods whose cords have been loosed.
t.4.17.3: When he, the lord of the hosts of vānaras, had fallen to the ground, the earth no longer shone, like the sky whose moon has vanished.
t.4.17.4: Even though that great-souled one had fallen to the ground, his body was not forsaken by splendour, nor by the breaths of life, nor by radiance, nor by valour.
t.4.17.5: That excellent golden garland, adorned with jewels and given by Śakra, sustained the life-breaths, the splendor and the glory of the chief of the monkeys.
t.4.17.6: With that golden garland, the heroic leader of the monkey hosts looked like a rain-cloud whose edges are tinged by the glow of twilight.
t.4.17.7: His garland, his body, and the arrow that pierced his vital parts: through these, as though arranged in three ways, splendour shines upon him even though he has fallen.
t.4.17.8: That missile, shot from Rāma's bow, which opens the path to heaven, brought that hero to the supreme state.
t.4.17.9: Him, fallen thus in battle like a fire whose flames have died out, like Yayāti cast down from the world of the gods when his merit was spent,
t.4.17.10: Him, struck down upon the earth like the sun hurled down by Time at the end of an age, unassailable as the great Indra, irresistible as the great Indra.
t.4.17.11: Rāma, followed by Lakṣmaṇa, saw the fallen Vālin, son of the great Indra, wearing a golden garland, lion-chested and mighty-armed, with a blazing face and tawny eyes, and he approached him.
t.4.17.12: Seeing Rāghava and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, Vālī spoke words that were courteous yet harsh, and grounded in dharma.
t.4.17.13: Having slain one whose face was turned away, what merit have you gained, now that I, intent upon battle with another, have met my death because of you?
t.4.17.14: Rāma is nobly born, endowed with strength of character, full of splendour, and faithful to his vows; he knows compassion and is devoted to the welfare of his subjects.
t.4.17.15: “Compassionate, of great energy, knowing what is proper to the occasion, firm in his vows”: thus all beings on earth are proclaiming your fame.
t.4.17.16: Having weighed those virtues of yours and your noble lineage, I came to face Sugrīva, even though Tārā had forbidden me.
t.4.17.17: "You ought not to strike me while I am enraged and heedless, fighting with another": such was the thought that arose in my mind when I could not see you.
t.4.17.18: I did not know you for what you are: a man of ruined spirit, unrighteous, bearing the banner of dharma, yet sinful in conduct, like a well covered over with grass.
t.4.17.19: I did not recognize you for what you are: a sinner wearing the garb of the virtuous, cloaked in a disguise of righteousness, like a fire hidden from sight.
t.4.17.20: Since I do you no harm, either in your realm or in your city, and I do not defy you, why do you slay one who is without offence?
t.4.17.21: Me, a monkey who always lives on fruits and roots and roams the forest, who was not fighting against you here but was engaged in combat with another…
t.4.17.22: You are the son of a lord of men, renowned and pleasing to behold. You also bear an outward sign, O king, that is seen to be joined with dharma.
t.4.17.23: Who, born in a family of kṣatriyas, learned and freed from doubt, would commit a cruel deed while cloaked in the outward signs of dharma?
t.4.17.24: O Rāma, born in a royal family and renowned as righteous, why do you, who are base, go about in the guise of a noble man?
t.4.17.25: Conciliation, generosity, forbearance, righteousness, truthfulness, steadfastness and valour are the virtues of kings, O king, and so too is punishment for those who do wrong.
t.4.17.26: We are forest-dwellers, Rāma, beasts who live on roots and fruits; this is our nature, but you are a man, a lord of men.
t.4.17.27: Land, gold and silver are the causes for subduing another; so what greed could you have for the forest, or for my fruits?
t.4.17.28: Statecraft and discipline, and likewise punishment and favour: the conduct of kings is clearly defined, and kings do not act as their own desires dictate.
t.4.17.29: But you are ruled by desire, quick to anger and unsteady; your kingly conduct is confused, and you are devoted only to your bow.
t.4.17.30: You have no reverence for dharma, nor is your mind set upon artha; living by desire, you are dragged along by your senses, O lord of men.
t.4.17.31: O Kākutstha, having slain me here with an arrow, though I had done no wrong, what will you say in the midst of the virtuous, having committed so contemptible a deed?
t.4.17.32: The slayer of a king, the slayer of a brahmin, the killer of a cow, the thief, the one who delights in taking the life of living beings, the unbeliever, and the younger brother who marries before his elder brother: all these go to hell.
t.4.17.33: My skin may not be worn by the virtuous, and my hair and bone are shunned; my flesh, too, is not to be eaten by followers of dharma such as you.
t.4.17.35: O King, the wise do not touch my skin or my bones, and my flesh is not to be eaten; such am I, a five-nailed creature, and yet I have been slain.
t.4.17.34: O Rāghava, five five-nailed animals may be eaten by brahmins and kṣatriyas: the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the hare, and the tortoise as the fifth.
t.4.17.37: Deceitful, dishonest, base, falsely feigning a humble mind, how could a sinner like you have been begotten by the great-souled Daśaratha?
t.4.17.36: O Kākutstha, with you as her lord the earth is not truly protected, just as a virtuous young woman who has fallen to a scoundrel is left without a true protector.
t.4.17.38: I have been slain by Rāma, an elephant who has snapped the girth-rope of good conduct, who oversteps the dharma of the virtuous, and who has thrown off the goad of righteousness.
t.4.17.40: But I, who am hard to approach, have been struck down in battle by you while you remained unseen, like a man fast asleep, overcome by drink, who is bitten by a serpent.
t.4.17.39: But had you fought me in battle in plain sight, O son of a king, today you would be seeing the god Vaivasvata, slain by me.
t.4.17.41: Though I have been slain by you out of your desire to please Sugrīva, I could have bound Rāvaṇa by the neck in battle and handed him over to you unslain.
t.4.17.43: It is fitting that Sugrīva should obtain the kingdom when I have gone to heaven; but it is not fitting that I have been slain by you in battle through unrighteousness.
t.4.17.42: Even had Maithilī been placed in the waters of the ocean or in Pātāla, I would have brought her back at your command, like the white she-mule.
t.4.17.45: Having spoken thus, the great-souled son of the king of the immortals, his mouth parched and tormented by the blow of the arrow, gazed upon Rāma, who shone like the sun, and fell silent.
t.4.17.44: Granted, the world is yoked by Time to a fate of this kind; but if what you have brought about is proper, let a fitting answer be well thought out.
